title: Saul Looks for Donkeys and Finds Samuel
summary: Saul, the tall and handsome son of a wealthy Benjamite named Kish, goes searching for his father's lost donkeys. After days of fruitless wandering, his servant suggests consulting a man of God in a nearby town. The day before, the LORD had told Samuel that he would send him a man from Benjamin to anoint as leader. Samuel meets Saul, tells him the donkeys have been found, seats him in the place of honor at a sacrificial meal, and the next morning takes him aside to reveal the word of God.
story: In chapter 8 the LORD told Samuel to give the people a king, and Samuel sent everyone home. Chapter 9 tells how the king is found, and it begins not with a national search but with a farm errand. The contrast is deliberate. Israel asked for a king to fight its battles; God answers through a young man who can't find his father's donkeys and has to be told where to go by his servant. The chapter moves Saul, step by step and without his knowing it, toward the prophet and the anointing in chapter 10. It also introduces the man whose rise and fall will dominate the rest of 1 Samuel.
historical:
Saul belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, which occupied a small strip of land between Ephraim to the north and Judah to the south. Benjamin had nearly been wiped out in the civil war described in Judges 20-21, which may explain Saul's description of it as the smallest tribe. Choosing a king from Benjamin had political advantages, since it lay between the powerful northern and southern tribes. Saul's hometown, Gibeah, is traditionally identified with Tell el-Ful, just north of Jerusalem, though some scholars have proposed other sites.

The regions Saul passes through (Shalishah, Shaalim, and Zuph) can't all be located with certainty, though Zuph connects with Samuel's family, since Samuel's ancestor was named Zuph (1:1). The town where Saul meets Samuel is never named, and whether it was Ramah, Samuel's home, is debated. The quarter shekel of silver the servant offers reflects a time before coins, when payment was made by weighing out pieces of metal; the shekel was a unit of weight of roughly eleven or twelve grams.
cultural:
Consulting a seer or prophet about practical matters, like lost animals, was normal in the ancient world, and it was customary to bring a gift. The narrator's comment in verse 9 explains an older term, seer, for readers who knew only the later term, prophet; it is one of several clues that the book was written some time after the events. The high place (in Hebrew bamah) was a local open-air worship site, often on elevated ground. Before the temple was built in Jerusalem, sacrifice at such places was common and not condemned; only later, after the temple, did the Prophets and the books of Kings treat them as rivals to the central sanctuary and places of idolatry.

The sacrificial meal was a communal feast. The meat of a peace offering was eaten by the worshipers, and seating and portions reflected status. Samuel places Saul at the head of about thirty guests and gives him a reserved portion, the leg and what was attached to it. The right thigh was ordinarily the priest's portion (Leviticus 7:32), so this gesture singled Saul out in a way the guests would have noticed. Sleeping on a flat roof was common in the warm season, and the roof was also a private place for conversation.
literary: The chapter is a carefully paced story in which the reader knows more than Saul does. The narrator reveals in verses 15-17 what the LORD told Samuel the day before, so we watch Saul walk into God's plan without realizing it. Many scholars compare the story to a folktale pattern in which a young man sets out to find lost animals and finds a kingdom. Saul's character is sketched through small details. He is impressive to look at, a head taller than everyone, but passive: the servant has the ideas, the money, and the knowledge of the man of God. Key words return: find, used seven times (Saul can't find the donkeys, but the young women say he will find the seer), and seer, from the verb to see. Samuel's cryptic question in verse 20 about the desire of Israel hints at the kingship, and Saul's humble reply mirrors the protests of earlier leaders like Gideon (Judges 6:15).

outline.t: The lost donkeys and the servant's idea
The young women at the well direct them to the seer
The LORD had told Samuel in advance
Samuel meets Saul and hints at his future
Saul honored at the sacrificial feast
On the roof and at the edge of town

doctrines.note: Lost donkeys, a servant's suggestion, a coin in a pocket, young women at a well, a prophet leaving the gate just as Saul arrives: every ordinary detail turns out to serve God's purpose. The chapter shows God directing events through ordinary means, even when the people involved have no idea.

God chooses Saul and tells Samuel ahead of time. The people demanded a king, but the choice of who that king will be remains God's, as Deuteronomy 17:15 required. The king is given, not self-appointed.

The LORD reveals his plan to Samuel before the event, literally uncovering his ear, and Samuel then reveals the word of God to Saul. The chapter shows the prophet as the one who hears God's word and through whom it reaches the king.

words.note: Nagid, leader or ruler. God tells Samuel to anoint Saul as nagid, not melekh (king). Many scholars think nagid means something like ruler-designate or the one God has appointed, emphasizing that the leader is appointed by God and answerable to him. The same word is later used of David (13:14).

Mashach, to anoint, to pour or smear oil on someone. Anointing set a person apart for a special role, usually as priest or king. The noun mashiach, anointed one, comes from this verb. God commands Samuel to anoint Saul, which makes the king the LORD's anointed.

Ro'eh, seer, one who sees. The narrator explains that the prophet of the narrator's day was formerly called the seer. The word emphasizes that the prophet sees what others cannot, a fitting term in a chapter where Samuel sees Saul coming and knows who he is.

Matsa, to find. The chapter repeats it seven times. Saul can't find the donkeys, is told he will find the seer, and is told the donkeys have been found. The search for lost animals becomes the means by which God finds Saul.

christ: The chapter's link to Christ runs through the word anointed. God tells Samuel to anoint a leader who will save his people from the hand of the Philistines, because their cry has come to him. That language, a leader anointed by God to save his people because he has heard their cry, echoes the exodus and anticipates the later hope for the Messiah, the Anointed One. Saul will fail to be that leader, and the book shows why. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one anointed by the Spirit to bring good news and liberty (Luke 4:18), the Savior who fulfills what Israel's kings only partly and imperfectly embodied. The connection is one of pattern and vocabulary, not a prediction in this chapter.

hard.q: If God knew Saul would fail, why did he choose him?
hard.a: The question is natural, since the LORD will later reject Saul and say he regrets making him king (15:11, 35). Several answers have been given. Some stress that Saul was genuinely suited to the task in many ways (he was humble at first, received the Spirit, and won real victories), and that his failure came from his own choices, not from a defect in God's selection. Others see Saul as the kind of king the people asked for, impressive in appearance and a warrior, and read his reign as a lesson in the limits of choosing by outward appearance, contrasted later with David, chosen because God looks at the heart (16:7). Still others note that God's plan included both Saul's reign and its failure, preparing the way for David without excusing Saul's disobedience. These views can be held together. The Bible regularly presents God as sovereign over outcomes while holding people fully responsible for their decisions, and it doesn't claim to explain how the two fit.

questions: Saul's search for lost donkeys led to his anointing as king. Where have ordinary errands or detours in your life turned out to matter more than you knew?
Saul's servant had the idea, the knowledge, and the money. What does this chapter suggest about the people God uses who stay in the background?
Saul protests that he comes from the smallest tribe and the least clan. Is his humility here a strength, or does it hint at something that will cause trouble later?
